Historical observations for this pairing came from four research programs that have collected measurements consistently over the last few decades. Data come from two stations in the Atlantic Ocean (Bermuda and the Canary Islands), one in the Caribbean Sea (Cariaco Basin), and one in the Pacific (Hawaii). All four stations measure pH or other variables that can be used to calculate pH.

Model outputs are based on a set of seven global climate models that reflect scientists’ current understanding of how greenhouse gases warm the atmosphere; how this heat moves between the atmosphere, water, and land; and how changing concentrations of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere will affect ocean chemistry. These same seven models were part of the set of 16 used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. (The other nine models did not include pH.) The modeled lines are smoother than the historical trends because the project team averaged seven models together and also applied an 11-year smoothing filter, both of which smooth out year-to-year variability. Multi-year smoothing also eliminates the seasonal ups and downs that appear in the observed data. However, the shaded bands show monthly ranges without smoothing, so they show both year-to-year and month-to-month variability.

Climate models provide projections in the form of a gridded map. This pairing shows modeled pH for the grid cells where each of the four observation stations are located.
